post_text:
I assumed Kafka partition keys guaranteed chronological ordering across active consumer rebalances.

That misplaced confidence collapsed during peak traffic when out-of-order event delivery silently corrupted thousands of customer ledger balances.

I designed our payment pipeline using asynchronous event streams, trusting message arrival timestamps to keep creation events strictly ahead of debit events.

When a minor network blip triggered a consumer group rebalance, partition ownership shifted while messages were still in flight.

Debit events suddenly hit our workers before the corresponding account creation records existed, bypassing my validation checks.

I relied on the naive assumption that network arrival mirrors real-world causation. The database accepted the inverted operations because I trusted the transport layer to maintain state integrity instead of enforcing hard sequence boundaries at the persistence layer.

What I learned:

Distributed streams do not guarantee temporal reality, only message delivery.
lesson_extracted: Sequence order must be explicitly enforced by monotonic version numbers in the persistence layer, never implied by the transport mechanism.
